days.title: The Core Loop: Plan, Apply, Destroy

tasks.title: Change something and run plan without applying. Read every line of the proposed change.

Apply the change and compare the result to what the plan predicted.
Make a change that forces replacement rather than update, and spot it in the plan.
Run terraform fmt and terraform validate and make both part of your habit.

days.title: State: The Thing That Breaks People

tasks.title: Open the state file and find the resource you created inside it.

Use terraform state list and terraform state show to inspect tracked resources.
Break it: delete a resource in the console, then run plan and see what Terraform wants to do.

Reference one resource attribute from another and let Terraform work out the order.
Read how Terraform builds a dependency graph from those references.

Use terraform console to test expressions before putting them in your code.

Use a for expression to transform a list into the shape a resource needs.

Start an apply, open a second terminal, and watch the second one refuse to run.
Read what force unlock does and why it is dangerous to use casually.
Confirm bucket versioning gives you a recoverable history of the state file.
Change a resource in the console so it no longer matches your code.
Run plan and read exactly how Terraform describes the difference.
Decide whether to apply the code or update the code, then do it deliberately.

Create a small resource manually in the console.

days.title: Rebuilding The Network Layer In Code

questions.prompt: What is the main problem infrastructure as code solves?
options: Environments that can be rebuilt and reviewed instead of clicked together
questions.explanation: Code makes infrastructure repeatable, reviewable and recoverable, which clicking never is.

questions.prompt: What does terraform init do?
options: Prepares the directory and downloads the required providers
questions.explanation: It sets up the working directory before any planning or applying can happen.

questions.prompt: What does terraform plan do?
options: Shows what would change without changing anything
questions.explanation: Plan is the dry run, and reading it properly is the habit that prevents accidents.

questions.prompt: In a plan, what does the minus slash plus symbol mean?
options: The resource will be destroyed and recreated
questions.explanation: Replacement is the symbol worth watching for, because it means downtime or data loss.

questions.prompt: What is Terraform state?
options: A record mapping your configuration to real world resources
questions.explanation: Without state, Terraform has no way to know which real resource matches which code block.

questions.prompt: You delete a Terraform managed resource in the console. What does the next plan show?
options: That it needs to be created again
questions.explanation: Terraform compares reality to the configuration and proposes recreating what is missing.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid hand editing the state file?
options: It is easy to corrupt and there are commands designed for the job
questions.explanation: State commands exist precisely so you never have to open the file with an editor.

questions.prompt: How does Terraform usually work out the order to create resources?
questions.explanation: Referencing one resource from another creates an implicit dependency.

questions.prompt: When would you need depends_on?
options: When a dependency exists that Terraform cannot infer from references
questions.explanation: It is the escape hatch for relationships that are real but invisible in the configuration.

questions.prompt: What does terraform validate check?
options: That the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent
questions.explanation: It catches configuration errors before you attempt a plan against the provider.

questions.prompt: In what order does Terraform destroy resources?
options: The order they appear in the file
questions.explanation: Dependents are removed before the things they depend on.

questions.prompt: Why pin a provider version?
options: So a new provider release cannot change behaviour unexpectedly
questions.explanation: Unpinned versions turn a working configuration into one that can break without you changing anything.

questions.prompt: Running plan makes changes to your infrastructure.
questions.explanation: Plan only reads and reports, which is why it is safe to run at any time.

questions.prompt: Terraform can manage resources across more than one cloud provider.
questions.explanation: Provider plugins are what make it cloud agnostic, unlike a single vendor tool.

questions.prompt: Reading the plan output carefully before applying is the single most important Terraform habit.
questions.explanation: Almost every serious Terraform accident was visible in a plan that nobody read.

questions.prompt: What should a variable declaration include beyond its name?
options: A type and a description at minimum
questions.explanation: Types catch mistakes early and descriptions make the configuration usable by other people.

questions.prompt: Which has higher precedence, a tfvars file or a value passed on the command line?
questions.explanation: Command line values sit at the top of the precedence order.

questions.prompt: What does marking a variable as sensitive do?
options: Stops it being displayed in command output
questions.explanation: It hides the value from output, but it does not encrypt it inside the state file.

questions.prompt: What is a data source used for?
options: Reading information about something Terraform does not manage
questions.explanation: Data sources let you look things up instead of hardcoding identifiers.

questions.prompt: Why look up an AMI with a data source instead of hardcoding the id?
options: Because AMI ids differ by region and change over time
questions.explanation: Hardcoded ids break the moment you change region or the image is updated.

questions.prompt: What is a locals block for?
options: Naming values computed once and reused across the configuration
questions.explanation: Locals reduce repetition and keep naming conventions consistent.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with using count over a list?
options: Removing a middle item shifts the indexes and causes unnecessary recreation
It cannot create more than ten
questions.explanation: Index based identity is fragile, which is exactly what for_each fixes.

questions.prompt: When is for_each the better choice?
options: When creating identical copies with no identity
When each instance has a stable key such as a name
When you need exactly one resource
questions.explanation: Keyed identity means adding and removing entries does not disturb the others.

questions.prompt: What does prevent_destroy do?
options: Makes Terraform refuse to destroy that resource
questions.explanation: It is a guardrail for things like a production database that must never be removed by accident.

questions.prompt: When does create_before_destroy help?
options: When replacing a resource without a gap in service
questions.explanation: The replacement is stood up before the old one is removed, which avoids downtime.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of using ignore_changes?
options: Real drift becomes invisible to Terraform
questions.explanation: You are telling Terraform to stop caring about an attribute, so changes there go unnoticed.

questions.prompt: What do provider default tags achieve?
options: Every resource is tagged consistently without repeating yourself
questions.explanation: Consistent tagging is what makes cost tracking and cleanup possible later.

questions.prompt: terraform console lets you test an expression before putting it into your configuration.
questions.explanation: It is the quickest way to check a function or interpolation without running a plan.

questions.prompt: A variable validation block can reject an invalid value before any resource is created.
questions.explanation: Failing early on bad input is much cheaper than failing halfway through an apply.

questions.prompt: A provider alias lets one configuration work with two regions at the same time.
questions.explanation: You define a second provider configuration and reference it explicitly where needed.

questions.prompt: Why is local state a problem for a team?
options: Only one person has it, and concurrent work overwrites or diverges
questions.explanation: Shared infrastructure needs shared state, otherwise two people manage two different pictures of reality.

questions.prompt: What should be enabled on an S3 bucket used for Terraform state?
questions.explanation: Versioning gives you a recovery path and encryption protects what is inside.

questions.prompt: What does the DynamoDB table provide in a Terraform backend?
options: A lock so two applies cannot run at once
questions.explanation: Locking prevents simultaneous applies from corrupting the shared state.

questions.prompt: Why is force unlock dangerous?
options: It can release a lock while another apply is genuinely still running
questions.explanation: Breaking a legitimate lock is how two applies end up racing each other.

questions.prompt: What is configuration drift?
options: Reality no longer matching the configuration
questions.explanation: Drift is what happens when someone changes things outside the tool.

questions.prompt: How do you detect drift?
options: Run plan and read what Terraform wants to change
questions.explanation: Plan compares the real world with your configuration, which is exactly what drift detection is.

questions.prompt: You find drift. What are your two legitimate options?
options: Apply the code to restore it, or update the code to match reality
questions.explanation: Either the code is right and reality should change, or reality is right and the code should be updated.

questions.prompt: What must you do before importing a resource?
options: Write the matching configuration for it
questions.explanation: Import only populates state, so without matching configuration the next plan wants to destroy it.

questions.prompt: What does terraform state mv do?
options: Changes which state address a resource is tracked under
questions.explanation: It is how you rename or restructure code without destroying and recreating the real resource.

questions.prompt: What does terraform state rm do?
options: Removes it from state while leaving it running
questions.explanation: The resource becomes unmanaged, which is useful when handing it to another configuration.

questions.prompt: What should you always do before state surgery?
questions.explanation: State operations are hard to undo, and a backup is the only real safety net.

questions.prompt: Why is importing a large hand built environment painful?
options: Every resource needs matching configuration written by hand first
State cannot hold that many resources
questions.explanation: The work is in writing accurate configuration for everything, not in the import command itself.

questions.prompt: State files should be committed to git so the team can share them.
questions.explanation: State often contains sensitive values and needs locking, which is why a remote backend is used instead.

questions.prompt: After a successful import, the plan should report no changes if your configuration matches.
questions.explanation: A clean plan is the proof that your code accurately describes the imported resource.

questions.prompt: Bucket versioning on the state bucket gives you a recoverable history of state.
questions.explanation: If an apply corrupts state, an earlier version is still available to restore.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of using a well maintained public module?
options: You inherit patterns and edge case handling you would otherwise get wrong
questions.explanation: Mature modules encode a lot of hard won detail that a first attempt usually misses.

questions.prompt: Why pin a module version?
options: So an upstream change cannot alter your infrastructure unexpectedly
It is required by the registry
questions.explanation: An unpinned module can change what it creates the next time you run init.

questions.prompt: What is the trade off of using a public module?
options: Less control and understanding of what is actually created
questions.explanation: Convenience comes at the price of a layer you did not write and may not fully understand.

questions.prompt: What makes a good module interface?
options: Clear inputs, useful outputs, and internals kept hidden
questions.explanation: A module should expose what callers need and hide the rest.

questions.prompt: Why write a README for your own module?
options: So someone else can use it without reading the source
questions.explanation: A module without documentation gets rewritten by the next person instead of reused.

questions.prompt: How should staging and production usually be separated?
options: Separate state, same modules, different variable values
questions.explanation: Reusing the code while isolating the state is what makes promotion safe and predictable.

questions.prompt: Why should staging be smaller than production?
options: To test the same code without paying production prices
questions.explanation: The shape should match while the size does not, and variables are how you do that.

questions.prompt: What is the correct promotion flow for a change?
options: Apply to production and roll back if needed
Apply to staging, verify, then apply the same code to production
questions.explanation: The same code proven in staging is what should reach production, unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why make the NAT gateway optional through a variable?
options: So cheaper environments can skip an expensive resource
It cannot be created in code
questions.explanation: Cost control through configuration is one of the practical wins of infrastructure as code.

questions.prompt: What should you do before applying a large plan?
options: Read it fully and count the resources it will create
questions.explanation: A large plan is exactly where an unnoticed replacement or deletion does the most damage.

questions.prompt: What does a successful destroy and rebuild from code prove?
options: That your environment is genuinely reproducible
questions.explanation: Reproducibility is the whole promise of infrastructure as code, and this is how you verify it.

questions.prompt: Which statement is strongest on a CV?
options: Rebuilt a full AWS environment from code and destroyed and recreated it in under an hour
questions.explanation: A demonstrated, timed outcome shows capability that a familiarity claim cannot.

questions.prompt: Using the same module for two environments with different inputs is a normal and recommended pattern.
questions.explanation: Shared code with environment specific values is how teams keep environments consistent.

questions.prompt: If your code is complete, you should be able to destroy everything and rebuild it without manual steps.
questions.explanation: Any manual step you still need is a gap in the configuration worth closing.

questions.prompt: Committing your Terraform configuration to a repository with a README turns it into portfolio evidence.
questions.explanation: Readable, runnable infrastructure code is one of the clearest signals of practical ability.
